rationale: The entry's distinguishing claim is that the biblical 'new moon' (chodesh, the day beginning the month) is in fact the FULL moon. The supplied evidence does not carry that identification better than the standard counter-reading. The book's whole case rests on two pillars: (1) reading Psalm 81:3's asyndetic pair 'new moon... keseh (full moon)... feast day' as one and the same day, and (2) reading Ezekiel 46:1's opened east gate as the full moon rising in the east at nightfall. Both pillars fail on the supplied texts themselves. Psalm 81:3 is naturally read as poetic enumeration of two festal moments in the same festal month — the trumpet at the month's beginning and the pilgrim feast at the full moon — which coheres with the fact that the solemn chag feasts fall mid-month, not on day one; the book's reading forces the feast day and month-start to coincide, which the verse does not state and which requires an undemonstrated wholesale calendar reconstruction that the chapter itself defers to another book. Ezekiel 46:1 opens the same east gate equally on every SABBATH, a weekly day with no fixed lunar phase; the gate opening therefore tracks sacred days for worship access, not the moon's position, and the book's astronomical reading cannot explain the sabbath half of its own proof-text. Proverbs 7:20 (keseh = full moon) establishes only that Hebrew has a word for the full moon; it does not equate keseh with chodesh. The remaining texts (1 Sam 20; Amos 8:5; Isa 66:23; Col 2:16-17) are phase-neutral and are explained identically or better by the conventional reading. Because the counter-reading explains every supplied detail — including the sabbath opening in Ezekiel 46:1 and the two-occasion structure of Psalm 81:3 — with fewer unsupported steps, and the book's core identification cannot explain the sabbath gate-opening without abandoning its own argument, the verdict is UNPERSUADED with no support for the core identification.
book_core_identification: That the 'new moon' — the phase marking the start of the biblical month — is the FULL moon (the light that enters at the east gate), rather than the dark conjunction or first crescent; this full-moon identification is the minimum proposition distinguishing the entry from the common interpretation.
book_secondary_elaborations: The new moon is 'the renewed moon,' the phase that marks the start of the month.
The full moon is pictured as entering 'in the east gate' (drawing on Ezekiel 46:1-3).
The new moon is the 'sign of the appointed times' (the moedim).
unsupported_glossary_assertions: The identification of the new moon as the full moon: Psalm 81:3's chodesh/keseh pair is better read as two distinct festal occasions (month-start trumpet and mid-month full-moon feast), and no supplied text states that the month begins at the full moon.

'The full moon in the east gate': Ezekiel 46:1 opens the same east gate on every sabbath, a day with no fixed lunar phase, so the gate-opening prescribes worship access on sacred days and does not identify the new-moon day with the full moon's eastern rising.
chapter_only_objections: The pearl-as-full-moon and bride-as-moon typology (Proverbs 3, Proverbs 31, Song of Songs 6:10) is an elaborate chapter-level construction not asserted in the entry and rests on many alternate lexical hearings (unpointed consonants, shanim/shnayim, halal as 'shine') stacked together.
The keseh/kisse' ('full moon'/'throne') wordplay and the Daniel 7 throne-room application are chapter-level and speculative.
The 'counterfeit moon' / thief-at-the-west-gate narrative contrasting sliver and full moon is homiletical, not exegetical.
The claim that the twelve pearl gates of Revelation 21 are twelve monthly full moons is unstated by any supplied text.
The full reconstructed calendar ('where the month truly begins, how the sabbaths fall') is explicitly deferred to a separate book and is unproven here.
strongest_counter_interpretation: The 'new moon' (chodesh) is the day beginning the lunar month, marked by the moon's renewal out of darkness (the conjunction/first visible crescent), observed with trumpet blasts and special offerings (Ps 81:3a; Num 10:10; 28:11-15), kept as a feast day in Israel's life (1 Sam 20:5, 18; Amos 8:5), continuing in prophetic visions of restored and perpetual worship (Ezek 46:1-3; Isa 66:23), and treated in the New Testament as a ceremonial shadow fulfilled in Christ (Col 2:16-17). In Psalm 81:3 the keseh (full moon) is a second, distinct festal moment — the mid-month pilgrim feast — named in poetic parallel with the new-moon trumpet of the same festal month.
counter_core_identification: The new moon is the month-opening observance at the moon's renewal from darkness (conjunction/crescent), a distinct day from the mid-month full-moon feast.
material_core_denial: The new-moon day and the full moon cannot be the same referent: if the month begins at the moon's renewal from darkness, the full moon falls mid-month (the day of the chag feasts), and Psalm 81:3 names two occasions, not one. Both identifications of the moon's phase at month-start cannot be true simultaneously.
counter_case: Psalm 81:3 naturally enumerates two festal moments — trumpet 'in the new moon' and 'at the keseh, on our solemn feast day' — matching the pattern of Numbers 10:10 (trumpets both at beginnings of months and at appointed feasts) and the Torah placement of the chag feasts on the 15th, the full moon; asyndeton in Hebrew poetry routinely lists distinct items, so the absence of 'and' does not merge the days.

Proverbs 7:20 shows keseh means the full moon, a mid-month marker (the husband away until then); it never equates keseh with chodesh, and Scripture consistently uses chodesh — the 'renewal' word — for the month's start, which fits the moon's reappearance from darkness, not its maximum.

Ezekiel 46:1-3 opens the east gate on both sabbaths and new moons; sabbaths fall at every lunar phase, so the opening marks sacred worship days for the prince and people, not the full moon's eastern rising; this uniform explanation covers both day-types where the book's astronomical reading covers only one.

1 Samuel 20:5, 18, Amos 8:5, Isaiah 66:23, and Colossians 2:16-17 all treat the new moon as a recognized calendrical observance without any statement about the moon's visible phase, and are fully explained by the conventional month-start reading.
book_explanatory_advantages: The book correctly observes that keseh in Psalm 81:3 lexically means the full moon and that the Hebrew lacks a conjunction between chodesh and keseh, a genuine textual detail many casual readers miss.
The east-gate imagery of Ezekiel 46 and the full moon's rising in the east at nightfall is an evocative correspondence.
The entry rightly ties the moon to the moedim as the appointed-time marker (Gen 1:14; Ps 104:19 background).
counter_explanatory_advantages: Explains Ezekiel 46:1's sabbath gate-opening, which has no lunar-phase correlation, under the same principle as the new-moon opening.
Explains Psalm 81:3's 'solemn feast day' (chag) coherently, since the pilgrim feasts fall mid-month at the full moon while trumpets also sound at month-beginnings — two moments in one festal month.
Coheres with the lexical sense of chodesh as renewal/reappearance after the moon's disappearance, without requiring a reconstructed calendar.
Accounts for every supplied text (1 Sam 20; Amos 8:5; Isa 66:23; Col 2:16-17) with no additional interpretive machinery.
evidence_book_core_cannot_explain: Ezekiel 46:1's opening of the same east gate on every sabbath: sabbaths fall at all lunar phases, so the gate-opening cannot signify the full moon entering the east; the book's own proof-text undercuts its astronomical reading, while the counter explains both day-types uniformly as sacred-day worship access.

Psalm 81:3's 'on our solemn feast day' (chag): the pilgrim chag feasts are mid-month observances distinct from the month's first day, so the verse's pairing of new-moon trumpet with full-moon feast is naturally two occasions; the book can merge them only by presupposing the very full-moon-month-start calendar it is trying to prove, a circular step the chapter itself defers to another book.
decisive_sources: Ezekiel 46:1-3 (east gate opened on sabbaths AND new moons — no lunar-phase correlation)
Psalm 81:3 (two festal moments in poetic parallel; chag feasts fall at mid-month full moon)
Proverbs 7:20 (keseh = full moon as a mid-month marker, cited in the chapter)
unresolved_objections: The precise force of the asyndeton in Psalm 81:3 remains genuinely debated; the book's one-day reading is possible, though not best-supported.

The supplied excerpts do not include Numbers 28:11-15 or Leviticus 23, so the mid-month placement of the chag feasts is background knowledge rather than a printed excerpt, slightly weakening the counter's documentary base within this bundle.
